lines.text: Grocery prices jumped 11.8% in 2022, then rose just 1.3% in 2023.
lines.say: Grocery prices jumped eleven point eight percent in twenty twenty-two, then rose just one point three percent in twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: So grocery inflation cooled a lot. But 1.3% is still up, on top of the 2022 jump.
lines.say: So grocery inflation cooled a lot. But one point three percent is still up, on top of the twenty twenty-two jump.

lines.text: Stack every year from 2020 to 2025, and groceries are up about 31%.
lines.say: Stack every year from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-five, and groceries are up about thirty-one percent.

lines.text: A $100 cart from late 2019 cost about $131 by late 2025.
lines.say: A hundred dollar cart from late twenty nineteen cost about a hundred thirty-one dollars by late twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Cooling inflation means prices rise more slowly. When prices actually fall, that's deflation, and it's rare for groceries.

post.title: Grocery inflation cooled. Your grocery bill didn't. Here's why.
post.ig:
Grocery inflation cooled. Your bill didn't.
BLS food-at-home prices: +11.8% in 2022, then +1.3% in 2023 (December to December). Slower, but still up.
From Dec 2019 to Dec 2025, groceries rose about 31%: a $100 cart became about $131.
Cooling inflation means prices rise more slowly; when prices actually fall, that's deflation, which is rare for groceries. Grocery prices were up 2.2% in the 12 months to Aug 2026.
Source: BLS Consumer Price Index.
